hints: Read the wording very carefully. Does it ask for the size of the image you see, or the real distance between the two structures on the slide?
Remember what magnification actually does: image size = actual size x magnification. Which part of that equation changes when you turn from x40 to x400, and which part stays the same?
walkthrough:
**Spot what is really being asked**

Great catch to pause here. The question says the structures *are* 200 nm apart. That is their real, actual separation on the specimen.

Magnification makes the image look bigger, but it never moves the real structures further apart.

**Apply the magnification rule**

Think of the friendly formula:
$$image\ size = actual\ size \times magnification$$

When you go from $\times 40$ to $\times 400$, the image size gets 10 times bigger. The actual size stays exactly the same.

**Conclude with confidence**

So the real distance is still $200\ nm$, even though it looks larger and more spread out at $\times 400$.

That is why we choose C. Do not be tricked into multiplying 200 nm by 10.

options.A: Incorrect. $2\ \mu m$ is $2000\ nm$, which is 10 times too big. This is the trap of multiplying the real distance by the 10-fold increase in magnification.
options.B: Incorrect. $20\ \mu m$ is far larger than the real separation and mixes up image size with actual size.
options.C: Correct. Magnification changes only the image size, not the real distance. The structures remain $200\ nm$ apart.
options.D: Incorrect. $2000\ nm$ is the same value as option A in different units, and again wrongly multiplies the actual distance by 10.
